summary:
They went silent. Now it’s your turn to listen, learn, and go where they went.

Silent Explorers brings forgotten space missions back to life through an interactive journey across the Moon and Mars. Explore six historic machines: Surveyor 3, Apollo 17 Moon Rover, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight.

The experience begins with immersive solar system storytelling, featuring mission slides, survival charts, and detailed dossiers covering timelines, scientific discoveries, and spacecraft hardware.

Go beyond reading by rotating and zooming authentic NASA 3D models, exploring their components, and driving Opportunity across simulated Martian terrain. Navigate using rover cameras, operate scientific instruments, and overcome challenges like dust storms.

Become a scientist through eight interactive experiments, evidence-based investigations, and hands-on activities that encourage critical thinking.

Discover landing sites through a mission atlas, explore authentic NASA photographs, and track achievements using a personal field journal with badges, scores, and saved progress.

With optional audio, accessible controls, mobile compatibility, and offline functionality, Silent Explorers makes space exploration engaging, educational, and accessible to everyone, without requiring an account.
details:
Silent Explorers – Project Details

Since the 1960s, NASA has left machines on other worlds, and no two of them ended the same way. Silent Explorers tells the story of six of them on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity and InSight. We built it for school-age space fans who want to know what these machines did and why it mattered.

What does it do and how does it work?

The site starts with a scrolling journey through the solar system that introduces each machine. From there, every mission gets its own page with a timeline, a big science question, and a guide to its parts, from rocker-bogie wheels to spectrometers to seismometers. Each page also shows how that machine’s story ended: left parked for good, buried in dust, or simply gone quiet after finishing its work. You can rotate and zoom official NASA 3D models, drive Opportunity across Mars with mast and navigation cameras, pick your instruments, and try to survive a dust storm. There’s also a first-person evidence-room lab, eight science activities (including Safe Landing, Find the Water and Power & Operations), real Apollo and Mars photographs, and a mission atlas of landing sites. A field journal keeps track of your badges, scores and progress.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We wanted students to do more than read. In the simulations they run into the same problems the robots did: not enough energy, rough terrain, and evidence that only supports careful conclusions. Seeing what each machine was built to find, like signs of ancient water on Mars, helps the science make sense. We hope it sparks curiosity and critical thinking, and keeps these missions from being forgotten.

Tools and Technologies

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D parts, Vite to build the site, and a service worker so the main content works offline. NASA’s public photographs and models are credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech. There’s no backend and no account needed, and we checked it with 81 automated tests plus browser testing in Chromium.

Creativity and Innovation

Most space websites tell you what happened. This one pairs a read-first story with simulation, so students learn the hardware by actually using it. Anything simulated or fictional is clearly labelled, so it’s always clear what is real NASA data and what is teaching material.

Factors Considered

We thought about scientific honesty, a smooth path from reading to understanding to doing, and accessibility, including reduced motion, optional audio and touch controls. We also cared about performance on ordinary devices. We chose to cover the Moon and Mars properly rather than touch on the whole solar system in a shallow way.
